_schema.purpose: Per-game memory map and reward weights, so training is generic across games instead of hardcoding one game's addresses in the code.
_schema.usage: train.py --game <id> reads the matching entry here for defaults. Any command-line flag overrides the file, so this holds the known-good baseline and experiments stay on the command line.

variables.source: 'info' = published by the stable-retro integration; 'ram' = one byte read directly; 'ram16' = little-endian pair (address + address_high << 8); 'ram_bcd3' = three digit bytes at address, address+1, address+2 combined as *100 + *10 + *1; 'unknown' = not located yet, shaping that needs it is inert.
variables.verified: true only when confirmed against recorded video with audit_ram.py. 'evidence' says how.

_schema.rewards: Weights applied by RewardShaper. Positive values pay, penalties are named as such and are subtracted.
_schema.finding_addresses: inspect_progress.py --demo (position), find_game_vars.py --find {coins,meter,timer} (counters/meters), find_ram_variable.py (any value that changes at a known moment), probe_after_death.py (game-state bytes). Always confirm with audit_ram.py against video before training.

SuperMarioBros3-Nes-v0.notes: Addresses below were located from human demo recordings and confirmed frame-by-frame against video. See KNOWN_BAD_ADDRESSES in train.py for addresses that were tried and disproven.

lives.evidence: decrements exactly at each on-screen death

score.evidence: published as one TENTH of the HUD value: a Super Mushroom (1000 on screen) reads +100, and a +100 on screen reads +10

screen_x.evidence: The LOW BYTE of level position, sweeping 0..255 and wrapping. Combined with the page counter 0x0075 it gives true level position -- see the 'progress' entry. Alone it is only useful for the first 256 pixels of a level, because it resets on every wrap.

powerup.evidence: tier changes on the exact frame a power-up is taken on video. NOTE it also clears to 0 on level exit and on death, which is why the power-down penalty is skipped when the episode is ending.

coins.evidence: live counter. 0x25A2 mirrors it for the HUD but lags: comparing the two showed 3 divergences with 0x2167 changing first.

pmeter.evidence: speed/P-meter. Value equals the number of bars filled (0..6), then jumps to 127 when the P indicator lights. 127 means FULL, which is the precondition for raccoon flight. Located by correlating with sustained run+direction input.

timer.evidence: three digit bytes at 0x05EE/0x05EF/0x05F0 = *100 + *10 + *1. Range exactly 0..299 with ZERO increases across a whole demo. The integration's own `time` info key reads something unrelated (constant 299, then 43) and must not be used.

course_clear.evidence: 0 for a whole run, 255 only while a course is ending. VERIFIED ON FOUR RECORDINGS: it rose at frames 5827, 7036, 5267 and 4205, and a frame rendered from the replay at each of those shows Mario touching the end-of-course card panel -- the exact moment the course is cleared. The COURSE CLEAR banner is drawn 98-118 frames (1.6-2.0s) LATER, so this is the earliest honest moment rather than the announcement. It returns to 0 when the world map loads, about 5.5s after it rises. It did NOT fire at any of the four pipe entries in those same recordings (frames 3063, 838, 4249, 3334), and did not fire through 175 frames of raccoon flight (5582-5757) that a rejected candidate mistook for an ending. 0x0559 (also 0/255) and 0x05F3 (0/129) mark the identical block to within one frame and corroborate it. REJECTED: 0x0687, a 0/1 flag that is set on every clear but was also set through that flight. Reading this instead of inferring a clear from position is not a refinement -- inference got it wrong in every recording checked: a pipe at frame 3063 was logged as a clear, and three genuine clears were logged as nothing at all.

progress.evidence: LEVEL POSITION = hpos + (ram[0x0075] << 8). hpos is the LOW byte and wraps at 256 (which is why it appears to jump 241 -> 3); 0x0075 is the page counter and ticked up on 13 of 13 forward wraps and down on 2 of 2 backward ones, while changing only 16 times across 4971 frames -- it moves at rollovers and nowhere else. Range 0..32 pages, about 8192 pixels of level. Two earlier readings of hpos were wrong: that it caps at 144 (that was Mario stuck against the first obstacle, not a camera limit) and that its wraps were garbage (on-screen x cannot wrap; only a position can). Tried and REJECTED as progress: 0x00CF (per-frame scroll delta, returns to 0 whenever movement stops), 0x053C (world-map counter, frozen during play).

playstate.evidence: Optional. A byte that is constant during normal play and different during the death sequence, used to end episodes at the moment of the hit and to exclude death-animation garbage from progress. Tried and REJECTED: 0x07F1 (cycles 5->0->8 every ~24 frames DURING play), 0x0749 (flips only ~19 frames before lives decrements, i.e. the END of the death sequence).

terms.note: New ground covered -- the main signal. progress is info16: the integration's hpos plus the page byte, because hpos alone flatlines at the scroll threshold.
Lives GAINED only; positive_only keeps a death from paying a huge negative here, since the terminal term already prices dying.
Read from 0x00C4, not inferred from position -- inference was measurably wrong.

rewards.terms_not_ported: stuck_penalty, backtrack_scale and speed_bonus need position HISTORY rather than a single-step delta, and auto_advance needs a wrapper. They remain only in train_smb3_legacy.py; the terms above cover progress, score, coins, lives, power, the course clear and death.

reward_scale_reasoning.calibrate_on_achievable_not_theoretical: The scale must make the progress an agent can ACTUALLY reach dominate, not the progress a perfect run would reach. Calibrating progress_scale against a full level (8447 units) gave 0.05, and measurement then showed why that fails: an early agent reaches the first pipe at ~120 units, worth only +6, against a 25-50 death penalty. debug_rewards measured STAND -55.9 vs RUN -46.1 -- a 9.8 margin, which the startup gate correctly rejects (it needs 20+). Death outweighed everything achievable by 8:1 and the difference between running and standing was noise.
reward_scale_reasoning.current_scale: progress_scale 0.25: reaching the first pipe (~120 units) pays ~30, a full traverse of a ~3400-unit level pays ~850, and one decision of running (4-20 frames at ~2px/frame) pays 2-10. The STAND-vs-RUN margin the startup gate measures halves with it, from ~60-65 to ~30-32, which still clears the 20 threshold -- re-run debug_rewards.py to confirm, because that margin is the floor this scale cannot go below. Progress deliberately no longer dominates every other term: at 0.5 it did, and that is what made collecting irrational.
reward_scale_reasoning.death_penalty: 25 is deliberately modest. Dying already forfeits all remaining progress -- the value function learns that on its own -- so the explicit penalty only needs to discourage recklessness early. Too large and the agent becomes risk-averse and stops attempting the jumps that clearing obstacles requires.
reward_scale_reasoning.the_unit_that_matters: One SECOND of running = 120px x progress_scale = 30 reward at the current 0.25. Every other weight should be set as 'how many seconds of forward motion is this worth', because that is the trade the agent actually faces: any detour costs running time plus death risk. Halving progress_scale doubles what every fixed-size event is worth in those units, which is the whole point of the change -- it is cheaper and safer than inflating the events themselves.
reward_scale_reasoning.event_ratios: Against that 30/second unit: coin 40 = 1.3 seconds, power 400 = 13 seconds (worth a real detour and real risk), life 100 = 3.3 seconds, death 25 = 0.8 seconds, clear 800 = 27 seconds. speed is 0 -- see the note on it. stuck_penalty 0.1 bleeds while standing, on top of the progress not being earned; it was halved alongside progress_scale so standing still costs the same in relative terms.
reward_scale_reasoning.why_the_agent_ignored_collectibles: It cleared level 1 by running and jumping and collected nothing -- correctly, given the weights at the time. A coin paid 4 against 60/second of running, i.e. 0.07 seconds: detouring for one cost more in lost progress than it paid, before counting the death risk. The agent was not failing to explore, it was optimising exactly what it was told. Collection weights are now set in seconds-of-running so a coin is worth about half a second and a mushroom about 2.5, which makes a short detour rational without making finishing optional (a full traverse plus clear is still ~5200 against ~1350 for collecting everything).
reward_scale_reasoning.collection_is_a_dial: These are a preference, not a correctness fix. Higher collection weights buy a completionist agent that plays slower and dies more; lower ones buy a speedrunner. Nothing here is wrong at either setting -- decide which agent you want and set the seconds-of-running accordingly.
reward_scale_reasoning.clear_bonus: 800, LOWERED from 3000. At 3000 the agent became a pure speedrunner and would not collect anything, and the reason is risk pricing rather than the coin weight. With gamma 0.999 a mid-level state was worth about 4000, so an action that raised death probability by 5% cost ~200 in expectation -- more than any coin could pay, and every coin in SMB3 means jumping into blocks and into airspace that holds enemies. Refusing to detour was the correct play. The note that used to sit here -- 'deliberately large: this is the objective, everything else is texture' -- is precisely what produced the speedrunner, and it was written without pricing the risk that collecting actually carries.
reward_scale_reasoning.lower_the_movement_weights_dont_raise_th: coin_bonus has been wrong in both directions (4 = ignored, 100 = camping in the opening) because coins are a FINITE LOCAL WELL: inflate them and hoovering the coin-dense opening outearns pushing into new ground, which is farming, not collecting. Progress and clear are the opposite -- they scale with the whole level. So the ratio is now shifted by halving progress_scale (0.5 -> 0.25) and cutting clear_bonus (3000 -> 800) while LEAVING coin and power weights alone. Same relative shift, no farmable pot. Arithmetic for a ~3400-unit level: traverse 850 + clear 800 = 1650 for a pure speedrun; all coins (~25) 1000 plus a power-up 400 = 1400 more, so collecting nearly DOUBLES a run's value instead of adding the 26 percent it added before. Mid-level downstream value drops to ~1200, so the same 5 percent death risk now costs 60 against gains of 40-400 -- positive expected value, which it never was at the old weights.
reward_scale_reasoning.verify_dont_trust: Re-run debug_rewards.py after ANY change here. These weights are arithmetic against measured distances, and the first attempt at that arithmetic was still wrong -- the gate is what caught it.
reward_scale_reasoning.auto_advance: On by default. Without it every episode restarts at World 1-1, so the agent's whole experience is one level and it dies immediately anywhere else -- which is exactly what was observed in level 2. With it, clearing a level leads into the next one and training covers several levels in a single run, with no per-level save states captured by hand. The map walking happens as raw emulator frames inside one step, so PPO never sees the map and no scripted action is credited to the policy.
reward_scale_reasoning.backtrack_scale: 0. Backtracking is already unprofitable without an explicit penalty: progress pays only for ground never reached before, so retracing earns nothing, and the time spent is time not earning forward progress. That opportunity cost is the honest disincentive. An added penalty double-charges it and blocks play the game requires -- chasing a mushroom that pops out of a block and slides away, or the sections that must be crossed leftward or upward. At the old 0.5, retrieving a mushroom ~100 units back cost 25 in penalty plus ~100 in forgone progress against a 150 payout: nominally worth it, but so thin that any death risk made abandoning the power-up correct. A coin was clearly not worth chasing at all. If the agent ever starts drifting backwards aimlessly, raise this to about 0.05 rather than back to 0.5.
reward_scale_reasoning.the_real_cost_of_a_detour: NOT lost progress. Detour and come back and you still cover the same ground for the same progress reward -- it simply arrives later. The actual cost is DISCOUNTING: everything still ahead is delayed, so a detour of D decisions costs R x (1 - gamma^D) where R is the reward remaining in the run. Mid-level R is around 3100 here, so at gamma 0.995 a ten-decision detour costs 153 while a coin paid 30 -- the agent skipped coins because skipping was correct, and no coin weight below 153 could have changed that. Raising gamma to 0.999 drops the same detour to 31. This is why collection kept failing to appear no matter how the collection weights were set: the binding constraint was the discount factor, not the reward.
reward_scale_reasoning.gamma: 0.999, an effective horizon of ~1000 decisions. Needed both for detours to be worth taking and because auto-advance makes episodes span several levels -- the old 0.99 default could not see to the end of one. Cost: returns have far more variance, so expect explained_variance to drop and value_loss to rise. If explained_variance falls below about 0.3, step back to 0.998.
reward_scale_reasoning.power_loss_is_asymmetric: Gaining a power-up pays the full power_bonus; losing one is charged only power_loss_scale of it (0.25). Symmetric charging was measured doing real damage: shaping/power read -400 per rollout while shaping/progress stayed under 130 for the same rollout, so a single hit erased roughly a hundred decisions of forward movement. The agent responded exactly as instructed -- ep_len_mean climbed to 633 while barely advancing, i.e. it stayed alive by refusing to commit. Taking a hit is also partly luck, unlike choosing to grab a mushroom, so the two should not be priced the same. Seeking power-ups stays strongly rewarded; losing one is now a setback rather than a catastrophe.
reward_scale_reasoning.coin_weight_was_overcorrected: coin_bonus has now been wrong in both directions. At 4 it was 0.07 seconds of running, so detours never paid and the agent ignored coins entirely. At 100 it was 1.7 seconds, and since the opening of a level is coin-dense, hoovering up ~20 of them banked 2000 for no skill and no risk -- better than pushing into unknown ground -- and the clock running out afterwards cost only 25. The agent stayed near the start forever because that genuinely was the best play. 40 puts a coin at 0.67 seconds: worth a short hop that is on the way, not worth camping for.

reward_notes.jump_bonus: Deliberately 0. Paying for the ACT of jumping is farmable -- a policy converged on jumping in place at the left screen edge, where the bonus minus the stuck penalty was risk-free income. Clearing an obstacle already pays through the progress it unlocks.
reward_notes.speed_bonus: NOW 0, and it should stay there unless the goal changes to speedrunning. It pays on each 6 -> 127 P-meter transition, and the meter drops whenever the player stops or lands badly, so it is REPEATABLE: several refills a level at 150 each. That is a direct, recurring subsidy for sustained rightward sprinting -- one refill outpaid nearly four coins -- and worse, stopping to collect anything breaks the sprint, so the bonus charges the agent for collecting on top of the detour cost. The old justification here ('filling it needs a long sustained sprint that random exploration almost never produces') was true only of an agent that could not yet sprint; once it learned to, this became its best income stream. Turn it back on only to teach raccoon flight, and expect collection to stop while it is on.
reward_notes.stuck_penalty: Must exceed any per-decision bonus, or stalling somewhere and farming that bonus becomes net-positive.

recipes._note: Multi-phase runs. games.json holds the baseline; a phase overrides on the command line and the next phase resumes from its checkpoint. Nothing here is automatic -- run the phases in order.

teach_collection.why: A trained speedrunner ignores coins and power-ups because they were priced far below the running time they cost: a coin at 4 against 60/second of forward motion is 0.07 seconds, so detouring lost more than it paid. It is NOT that the policy fails to sample detours -- at ent_coef 0.02 measured entropy was 2.21 of a 2.565 maximum, i.e. 86% of uniform, so it explores constantly. Magnitude was the problem, so inflate it temporarily, let the behaviour be learned, then restore normal weights and keep the skill.
teach_collection.phase_1_force: SUPERSEDED. This used --coin-bonus 100 --speed-bonus 150, and both are now understood to be counterproductive: coin 100 makes the coin-dense opening a farm, and any speed_bonus pays for the sprint that collecting has to interrupt. The baseline weights in this file already price collection correctly; the only lever still worth pulling for a converged speedrunner is entropy, --ent-coef 0.03, so the policy samples detours often enough to discover they now pay.
teach_collection.phase_2_restore: Not needed once phase 1 is just an entropy bump: there are no inflated weights to restore. Resume the same run at the default --ent-coef once collection appears in the shaping ledger, so the policy sharpens around the behaviour instead of continuing to sample randomly.
teach_collection.watch_for: If phase 1 stops finishing levels, coin totals have overtaken the clear bonus: halve --coin-bonus. If phase 2 immediately reverts to ignoring everything, phase 1 was too short to consolidate; run it longer rather than raising the weights further.

patience_not_speed.why: There is no time penalty in this config -- time_penalty and survival_tick are both 0, so nothing charges the agent for taking longer. What still makes it impatient is DISCOUNTING: at the default gamma 0.99 the effective horizon is about 100 decisions, so a reward 300 decisions away retains only 5% of its value. A detour delays future progress, and heavily discounted future progress makes the detour look bad no matter how the collection weights are set. That is a property of the optimiser, not of the reward.
patience_not_speed.what_to_change: Raise --gamma. 0.995 doubles the horizon to ~200 decisions (a reward 300 away keeps 22%); 0.999 extends it to ~1000 (keeps 74%). This matters more now that auto-advance makes episodes span several levels: a 100-decision horizon cannot even see to the end of one level.
patience_not_speed.cost: Higher gamma makes value estimation harder -- returns have more variance and explained_variance typically drops. 0.995 is a safe step; go to 0.999 only if value_loss and explained_variance stay reasonable.
patience_not_speed.note_on_coin_weight: Raising coin weight makes coins more attractive but is exploitation, not exploration -- it does not send the agent anywhere new by itself. It does compound, though: stronger reinforcement when a coin is found means more coin-seeking, which visits more places where coins are. Entropy is the direct exploration lever, gamma is the patience lever, and coin weight is the value lever. They do different jobs.

training.notes: Actions carry their own hold length because for this game it is part of the move: (['A'],6) is a short hop and (['A'],20) a full jump. Episode end comes from the integration's own scenario (this is a standard integration), so no episode_end is declared.

_template.notes: Copy this for a new game. Set every address you can verify; leave the rest as 'unknown' and the matching shaping stays inert rather than reading garbage. Start with: python audit_ram.py --demo <recording> to see what the integration already publishes.

progress.evidence: find with inspect_progress.py --demo; it must climb the whole level and NOT reset when the player stops or backs up

TetrisTime-Nes-v0.notes: HUD is a DISPLAY-TILE buffer: one digit per byte, byte = digit + 0x30, most-significant digit first. Found by a known-value search over a recording and verified against the on-screen HUD at 9 frames.

score.evidence: 6 digit-tiles MSD-first; decoded == HUD SCORE at frames 3613/9034/14454/18068 (19/405/6411/6803) and every other sampled frame.

lines.evidence: 3 digit-tiles MSD-first; == HUD LINES at all sampled frames (0,2,7,12,18,21,30,31,39). A jump in this count is a line clear; +4 is a Tetris.

level.evidence: 2 digit-tiles; == HUD LEVEL (0->1). A binary copy also sits at 0x01E3.

game_over.evidence: A game-state enum: 0 before play, 0xF0 (240) for ALL active play, 0xF1 (241) at game over. In the top-out recording (studio_out/20260908-012346_tetris-time) it holds 240 through play and flips to 241 at frame 2480 (00:41.3, the exact frame the tile score at 0x0418 freezes and the piece stops falling), then holds 241 to the end. In a SECOND recording that clears level 0 into level 1 and plays on without topping out (studio_out/20260907-231546_tetris-time) it is a steady 240 for 17000+ frames across BOTH level transitions and NEVER reaches 241 -- so 241 is game-over specific, not per-level. Found with tools/find_game_vars.py --find-latch --after 2400 --control <the second recording>: the --control cross-check dropped 124 of 151 single-recording candidates whose latched value also occurs in a run that never ended. Test: game over when 0x0631 == 241 (equivalently 240->241). CORRECTION: an earlier version recorded 0x03B7 (1 in play, 0 at this top-out), but the second recording proved 0x03B7 is level parity -- it is 1 on level 0 and 0 on level 1, flipping at the level transition, not at game over. It was verified on only one recording, where the top-out happened to be on level 0, so game-over and level-0-end were indistinguishable. REJECTED here: 0x0258 (a post-game-over counter that ramps 0->1->2) and 0x063A (steps 0->224->230, two-stage, not a clean flag).

level_transition.evidence: 1 ONLY while the level-change animation runs, 0 during play. In the 1-player run studio_out/20260907-231546 (19875 frames) it is 0 for every frame except a single run, frames 13870-14596, which starts one frame after the level tile 0x042C goes 0->1 at 13869 and covers the clear bonus (score 811->4931). It does NOT fire at game over: across the whole top-out run studio_out/20260908-012346 it is 0 at every frame. Rejected 0x0029, 0x03F1, 0x0520 and 0x0524, which mark the same window but also trip during boot/menu. USE: while this is 1 the game is animating, not being played -- do not count it as play time, do not shape reward from it, and do not read a top-out from it.

TetrisTime-Nes-v0.two_player_notes: The 2-player HUD is ONE shared tile block. PLAYER 1 IS THE LEFT COLUMN and keeps the same addresses the game uses in 1-player; PLAYER 2 IS THE RIGHT COLUMN and follows each P1 field. Layout: 0x0418 P1 score (6) / 0x041E P2 score (6) / 0x0424 gap / 0x0425 P1 lines (3) / 0x0428 gap / 0x0429 P2 lines (3) / 0x042C P1 level (2) / 0x042E P2 level (2). Raw per-player line counters also sit as an adjacent pair: 0x006C P1, 0x006D P2. The P1=left / P2=right mapping is confirmed by the owner and consistent across both runs (run 1: P1 10/1 left, P2 21/2 right; run 2: P1 level 5 left, P2 level 8 right). These addresses were only findable after fixing the tools replay bug in f970f5b.

score_p1.evidence: Digit tiles, MSD first, byte = digit + 48. Verified on TWO independent 2-player runs: studio_out/20260908-193739_tetris-time at 7 frames, and studio_out/20260909-001721_tetris-time (P1 started level 5, P2 level 8) where a frame rendered straight from the replay reads "486 SCORE 1134 / 2 LINES 0 / 5 LEVEL 8" and every address decodes exactly that. Decoded 10,20,26,51,64,89,166 (run 1) and 486 (run 2) == on-screen P1 (left) SCORE.

score_p2.evidence: Digit tiles, MSD first, byte = digit + 48. Decoded 21,29,41,45,85,283,323 (run 1) and 1134 (run 2) == on-screen P2 (right) SCORE.

Decoded 1,1,2,3,3,3,3 (run 1) and 2 (run 2) == on-screen P1 LINES. Raw counter 0x006C agrees.

level_p2.evidence: Digit tiles, MSD first, byte = digit + 48. Verified on TWO independent 2-player runs: studio_out/20260908-193739_tetris-time at 7 frames, and studio_out/20260909-001721_tetris-time (P1 started level 5, P2 level 8) where a frame rendered straight from the replay reads "486 SCORE 1134 / 2 LINES 0 / 5 LEVEL 8" and every address decodes exactly that. Reads 8 in run 2, matching P2 chosen level 8. This settles an earlier ambiguity: the P2 level is 0x042E, NOT 0x042F (0x042F straddles the field and decodes 80).

lines_p1_counter.evidence: Raw byte line counter for P1; exact match at all 7 frames of run 1.

lines_p2_counter.evidence: Raw byte, adjacent to P1 counter; exact match for P2 at all 7 frames of run 1.

game_over_p1.evidence: Pure boolean per-player alive flag, an adjacent pair mirroring the lines counters at 0x006C/0x006D. On studio_out/20260908-193739 (fixed 2-player replay) both read 1 from frame 373 (play starts) and drop to 0 exactly at that player.s top-out -- 0x004A at frame 9262 and 0x004B at 8634, matching where each player.s score tiles freeze (204 and 323) -- with no flicker after. Only 0/1 ever observed. The P1 and P2 candidate sets shared no address, so these are per-player, not a shared flag. 0x004A is P1 (left).

On studio_out/20260908-193739 (fixed 2-player replay) both read 1 from frame 373 (play starts) and drop to 0 exactly at that player.s top-out -- 0x004A at frame 9262 and 0x004B at 8634, matching where each player.s score tiles freeze (204 and 323) -- with no flicker after. The piece struct is adjacent P1/P2 pairs, the same convention as the lines counters at 0x006C/0x006D. Climbs as the piece falls and resets on spawn; reset coincided with P1 locking at frame 127.

The piece struct is adjacent P1/P2 pairs, the same convention as the lines counters at 0x006C/0x006D. Same, for P2: reached 19 then reset to 4 at frame 80 when a new P2 piece spawned.

two_player.WELL_HEIGHT_OPEN_QUESTION: PARTLY RESOLVED. The two blocks at 0x0600 and 0x0700 are NOT mirrors of one board: each lock writes to exactly one of them, alternating, so taking whichever held more cells (the old behaviour) silently dropped every piece that landed in the other. read_well now unions them, which grows on every lock where either block alone stalls. STILL OPEN: the piece row counter reaches 21 while each block decodes 13 rows, and locks add only 2-3 cells rather than 4, so part of the board is still not being read -- most likely rows above the 13. Resolve before building a grid observation; the holes/height shaping is improved by the union but may still not see the very top of the stack.

training.start_state_notes: integrations/TetrisTime-Nes-v0/level0_1p.state -- a 1-player game already underway at level 0 (score 0, lines 0, first piece falling), so training never has to drive the boot screen and menus. Captured from studio_out/20260908-012346 at frame 1515, chosen because 0x0631 first reads 240 (playing) at frame 1485. Load with retro.make(state=level0_1p).
training.start_state_2p_notes: integrations/TetrisTime-Nes-v0/level0_2p.state -- a TWO-player game already underway at level 0 (both players alive, all counters 0), captured at frame 433 of studio_out/20260908-193739. Train the bot as PLAYER 2 from this state: it then learns on exactly the screen and controls it will use at deploy time, so there is no 1P->2P transfer problem. VERIFIED: loading it with players=2 and driving only the P2 half of the 18-bit action (bits 9..17) changes ONLY the right half of the screen (left-half pixel delta 0, right-half 125792). P1 can be left idle; its play does not affect P2 reward.
training.controls: Per player slice, buttons are [B, -, SELECT, START, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, A]: LEFT/RIGHT move the piece, DOWN soft-drops it, A rotates clockwise (B counter-clockwise is removed from action_set to streamline exploration). P2 occupies bits 9..17 of the joint action.
training.start_state_8_2p_notes: integrations/TetrisTime-Nes-v0/level8_2p.state -- a two-player game underway with P2 on LEVEL 8 (P1 on level 5), captured at frame 1800 of studio_out/20260909-001721. PREFER THIS FOR TRAINING: at level 0 gravity is ~960 frames per piece, so a random policy survived 1500 steps (6000 frames) without even topping out; from level 8 the same policy tops out in 288 steps with a genuinely full board (holes 10, height 63). Roughly 5x more complete episodes per frame, and a real learning signal.
training.well: P2 board at 0x0600/0x0700 + 16*row + 8 (P1 at +0), 13 rows x 10 columns, FOUR BITS per cell, dropping 3 wall nibbles each side; 0 = empty. Found by driving only P2 and watching which half filled. DOUBLE BUFFERED across 0x0600 and 0x0700 and the game alternates which is current, so read both and take whichever holds more filled cells -- a stale buffer lags behind, never ahead. Holds LOCKED cells only; the falling piece is not in it.
training.soft_drop: DOWN increases gravity and earns drop points. It is IGNORED when held across a piece spawn, so a policy has to re-press it per piece -- measured: DOWN held for 1200 frames landed no more pieces than no input at all, while a fresh press drops a piece within ~60 frames.

grid.mask_why: The falling piece is drawn into the sampled board, so the gap under it reads as holes that appear and vanish as it descends -- measured at +-8 per step on the holes term against a terminal of -10. It is masked out using its RAM row/column. The offsets were calibrated by diffing consecutive frames, since the cells a falling piece VACATES are exactly the piece: ramRow 10 -> grid row 5, ramCol 7 -> grid cols 4..6, hence row-5 and col-3.
grid.bounds_why: y=56 with 20 rows, NOT y=48 with 22. Verified against an EMPTY board, which must read as entirely empty: at y=48 the top sampled row picked up border/HUD bleed, so those columns read as filled at the top and every empty cell beneath them counted as a hole -- an empty board reported 120 holes and height 136. Row 21 was the well FLOOR, not blocks, which gave every column a permanent base height. The shaping was therefore dominated by artifacts and the handful of real holes were lost in them. y=56 stays aligned to the ROM 8-pixel block grid and covers y56..215, excluding both. row_offset moves 5 -> 6 because the grid origin dropped by one row.

observation.grid_why: The board is sampled from the RENDERED frame, one probe per cell. The RAM well layout could not be mapped: the blocks at 0x0600/0x0700 are neither mirrors nor halves, the best stride/base decode reproduced 3 of 22 rows against the screen, and any 13-row read compresses a stack that is really 22 rows. Sampling the drawn cells agrees with the screen by construction. x153 y48 cell 8 covers P2 well: 10 columns and 22 rows of 8-pixel tiles.
observation.why_not_pixels: Raw pixels were tried and did not learn. Three fixes -- cropping to P2, keeping the aspect square, and reading the whole board -- left survival flat at about 1500 frames across 1.5M+ timesteps. A CNN has to rediscover that the blobs form a 10-wide grid before it can learn placement; handing it the grid removes that problem. The observation is the board flattened plus the piece being placed (type one-hot, rotation, column, row), because the piece is not part of the board.

training.use_data_json_why: This integration was made by hand: data.json is {"info": {}} and scenario.json declares no done and no reward, so retro has nothing to contribute -- info is always empty and its done never fires. Everything real comes from this file instead: RAM variables for values and episode_end (game_over_p2 == 0) for the ending. Leaving it on would only be misleading.

feature_gate.why: Board features are recomputed only when the piece row DROPS -- a new piece spawning, meaning the previous one has locked -- and held constant in between. Sampling the board every step includes the falling piece, and the gap beneath it reads as holes that appear and vanish as it descends: measured, the holes term swung by +-8 PER STEP against a terminal of -10, so one step of that noise outweighed dying and the agent was graded on where a piece happened to be mid-air. Survival fell from ~1480 frames to ~1288 when the 22-row board was introduced without this.

training.release_frames_why: One frame of every decision is spent with no buttons held, so each decision is a fresh PRESS. Without it two identical decisions in a row reach the game as one sustained press: measured, repeated LEFT presses moved the piece 7,6,6,5,5,4 -- half did not register -- and a long hold triggers auto-repeat and skips columns. With one release frame the same four frames give a clean 7,6,5,4,3, one column per decision. This is why the bot could only slide pieces to a wall and never nudge one over a gap.

terms.note: A Tetris of four lines is worth far more than four singles, which a flat per-line rate cannot express.

Paid once per piece LANDED (the row counter resetting for the next piece). Without it the shaping was net-negative per piece with no achievable positive: every piece costs ~1.5 in holes while surviving paid 0.001 a step, so playing longer only accumulated penalty and the best available policy was to top out sooner. Observed exactly that -- survival fell from 303 to ~200 decisions during training. At 1.5 against holes at -0.5, a piece that opens no hole is worth +1.5, one hole +1.0, and three holes breaks even, so placing WELL is what pays rather than placing less.

Deliberately small. Soft-dropping earns drop points, and one careless episode banked 2088 of them; at 0.01 that is +21 and swamps the -10 for dying, teaching the bot to slam pieces down and ignore where they land.
